seljuk-empire.name: Seljuk Empire
seljuk-empire.summary: A medieval Turco-Persian empire founded in 1037 by brothers Tughril and Chaghri, stretching from Anatolia to Central Asia, whose 1071 victory at Manzikert weakened Byzantine control there.

arabia-felix.name: Arabia Felix
arabia-felix.summary: Latin name meaning 'Fertile Arabia' that ancient geographers used for South Arabia, roughly corresponding to modern Yemen.

ibn-battuta.name: Ibn Battuta
ibn-battuta.summary: A Maghrebi Muslim traveller and scholar (1304–1368/69) from Tangier who journeyed about 117,000 km across Africa, Asia and the Iberian Peninsula and dictated an account of his travels, the Rihla.

aden.name: Aden
aden.summary: Ancient port city on Yemen's south coast, at the eastern approach to the Red Sea, serving since 2014 as the de facto capital of Yemen's internationally recognized government.

cisterns-of-tawila.name: Cisterns of Tawila
cisterns-of-tawila.summary: A historic system of connected stone tanks in Aden, Yemen, built to collect rainwater for drinking and to protect the city from flooding.

rasulid-dynasty.name: Rasulid dynasty
rasulid-dynasty.summary: Sunni Yemeni dynasty that ruled Yemen from 1229 to 1454.

mufti.name: Mufti
mufti.summary: An Islamic jurist qualified to issue nonbinding legal opinions, or fatwas, on points of Islamic law, a role tracing back to the Quran and early Islamic communities.

al-afdal-al-abbas.name: Al-Afdal al-Abbas
al-afdal-al-abbas.summary: Ruler of Yemen's Rasulid dynasty from 1363 to 1377 who compiled a multilingual dictionary and cracked down on extortion by port officials to keep Yemen attractive to foreign traders.

arwa-al-sulayhi.name: Arwa al-Sulayhi
arwa-al-sulayhi.summary: Long-reigning ruler of Yemen from 1067 to 1138, the last of the Sulayhid dynasty and the first woman given the title Hujjah in Isma'ili Islam.

great-mosque-of-sanaa.name: Great Mosque of Sanaa
great-mosque-of-sanaa.summary: One of the oldest mosques in the world, said to have been founded around 633 CE in Sanaa, Yemen, built partly from materials taken from an earlier palace and church on the site.

great-mosque-of-zabid.name: Great Mosque of Zabid
great-mosque-of-zabid.summary: A historic congregational mosque in the old city of Zabid, Yemen.

ayyubid-dynasty.name: Ayyubid dynasty
ayyubid-dynasty.summary: A Sunni Muslim dynasty of Kurdish origin founded by Saladin in 1171, which ruled Egypt and much of Syria until its own Mamluk soldiers overthrew it in 1250.

zabid.name: Zabid
zabid.summary: One of the oldest towns in Yemen, on its western coastal plain, and a former capital of several ruling dynasties; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993.

al-ibn-al-asan-al-khazraj.name: al-Khazraji
al-ibn-al-asan-al-khazraj.summary: Yemeni historian (1331–1410) who worked for the Rasulid dynasty, also known as Ibn Wahhas.

taiz.name: Taiz
taiz.summary: A city in the Yemeni highlands near the Red Sea, the capital of Taiz Governorate and, as of 2023, Yemen's third largest city.

fatimid-caliphate.name: Fatimid Caliphate
fatimid-caliphate.summary: An Isma'ili Shia caliphate ruling North Africa and West Asia from the 10th to 12th centuries CE, claiming descent from Muhammad's daughter Fatima, with Egypt as its eventual centre.

ashrafiya-mosque.name: Ashrafiya Mosque
ashrafiya-mosque.summary: A historic madrasa-mosque in Taiz, Yemen, built in stages between roughly 1295 and 1400 and considered one of the city's most important Islamic monuments.

qarmatians.name: Qarmatians
qarmatians.summary: An Isma'ili Shia militant movement centred in eastern Arabia from 899 CE, notorious for sacking Mecca in 930 CE and stealing the Black Stone.

abbasid-caliphate.name: Abbasid Caliphate
abbasid-caliphate.summary: The third Islamic caliphate, ruling from 750 to 1258 with Baghdad as its capital for most of that time, known for ushering in the Islamic Golden Age of science and culture.

abu-al-bahlul-al-awwam.name: Abu al-Bahlul al-Awwam
abu-al-bahlul-al-awwam.summary: Shiite leader of the Abdul Qays tribe in Bahrain who overthrew Ismaili Qarmatian rule of the islands around 1058 and founded the village of Al-Awamiyah.

awal.name: Awal
awal.summary: An ancient name for Bahrain used for about eight centuries, derived from a pre-Islamic deity worshipped by the islands' inhabitants.

banu-amir.name: Banu Amir
banu-amir.summary: An ancient Arab tribe from western Arabia that dominated Najd after the rise of Islam and produced several renowned pre-Islamic poets.

abd-al-qays.name: Abd al-Qays
abd-al-qays.summary: An ancient Arabian tribe from Eastern Arabia, from which most of the Baharna people today descend.

uyunid-dynasty.name: Uyunid dynasty
uyunid-dynasty.summary: An Arab dynasty of the Banu Abdul Qays tribe that ruled Eastern Arabia for 163 years, from the 11th to 13th centuries, after seizing it from the Qarmatians.

abdullah-bin-ali-al-uyuni.name: Abdullah bin Ali Al Uyuni
abdullah-bin-ali-al-uyuni.summary: Founder and emir of the Uyunid Emirate, ruling from 1074 to 1107, who removed the Qarmatians from Eastern Arabia.

banu-muharib.name: Banu Muharib
banu-muharib.summary: An Arab tribe during Muhammad's era that was raided after intelligence of a planned attack near Medina, later settling in Kufa after the Muslim conquest of Iraq.

qatif.name: Qatif
qatif.summary: One of the oldest settlements in Arabia, with a history dating to 3500 BC, historically known to the Sumerians as Dilmun and now part of Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province.

malik-shah-i.name: Malik-Shah I
malik-shah-i.summary: Third sultan of the Seljuk Empire from 1072 to 1092, under whom the empire reached its peak, though real power lay with his vizier Nizam al-Mulk.

al-ahsa-governorate.name: Al-Ahsa
al-ahsa-governorate.summary: A governorate in eastern Saudi Arabia, historically called Hajar, the largest in the country by area, with Hofuf as its seat.

ibn-khaldun.name: Ibn Khaldun
ibn-khaldun.summary: An Arab Tunisian scholar and historian (1332–1406), best known for the Muqaddimah, a foundational work in historiography, sociology and economics.

muqaddimah.name: Muqaddimah
muqaddimah.summary: A 14th-century Arabic treatise by Ibn Khaldun on historiography, sociology and the philosophy of history, written in 1377 and sometimes seen as an early work of social science.

imru-al-qais.name: Imru' al-Qais
imru-al-qais.summary: Pre-Islamic Arabian poet from Najd, active in the late 5th and early 6th centuries and the last king of Kinda, often called the father of Arabic poetry.

qasida.name: Qasida
qasida.summary: An ancient Arabic ode form using a single meter and rhyme throughout, originating in pre-Islamic poetry and later adopted into Persian and Turkish literature.

ibn-arabi.name: Ibn Arabi
ibn-arabi.summary: An Andalusian Sufi mystic, poet and philosopher (1165–1240) whose vast writings, especially on the 'unity of existence,' became a dominant framework across the Muslim world.

al-andalus.name: Al-Andalus
al-andalus.summary: The Muslim-ruled territories of the Iberian Peninsula from 711 to 1492, which at their height covered all of Spain and Portugal, with Córdoba becoming a leading cultural and scientific center.

al-futuhat-al-makkiyya.name: Meccan Revelations
al-futuhat-al-makkiyya.summary: Major work of the philosopher and Sufi Ibn Arabi, written between 1203 and 1240. It sets out his spiritual journey, theology, metaphysics and mysticism in prose and poetry, with autobiographical elements.

mehmed-ii.name: Mehmed II
mehmed-ii.summary: Ottoman sultan (1432–1481), known as the Conqueror, who captured Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire, and expanded Ottoman rule across Anatolia and the Balkans.

maqamat-al-hariri.name: Maqamat al-Hariri
maqamat-al-hariri.summary: Collection of fifty tales written around the late 11th or early 12th century by al-Hariri of Basra, a Seljuk Empire official. Over a hundred manuscripts survive, thirteen of them illustrated.

yahya-ibn-mahmud-al-wasiti.name: Yahya ibn Mahmud al-Wasiti
yahya-ibn-mahmud-al-wasiti.summary: 13th-century Iraqi-Arab painter and calligrapher. He was both scribe and illustrator of a copy of al-Hariri's Maqamat dated 1237 CE, now in the Bibliothèque Nationale de France.

al-zamakhshari.name: Al-Zamakhshari
al-zamakhshari.summary: Medieval Muslim scholar of Iranian descent (1074–1143), a Mu'tazilite theologian, linguist and poet. He settled in Mecca for five years and became known as 'Jar Allah' (God's Neighbor).

al-kashshaaf.name: Al-Kashshaf
al-kashshaaf.summary: Influential 12th-century commentary on the Qur'an by Al-Zamakhshari, famous for its deep linguistic analysis. It is criticized for including Mu'tazilah philosophical views.

abd-al-qahir-al-jurjani.name: Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani
abd-al-qahir-al-jurjani.summary: Persian scholar of the 11th century, based in Gorgan, and one of the greatest literary theorists of medieval Islam. His two masterworks helped establish Arabic rhetoric as an independent science.

ibn-al-farid.name: Ibn al-Farid
ibn-al-farid.summary: Arab Sufi poet (1181–1234), born and died in Cairo. His poetry was admired across Arabic and Persian speaking regions, and Persian poets such as Jami wrote commentaries on it.

siege-of-baghdad.name: Siege of Baghdad (1258)
siege-of-baghdad.summary: The 1258 Mongol assault on Baghdad led by Hulegu, which killed the Abbasid caliph and hundreds of thousands of residents and is traditionally seen as ending the Islamic Golden Age.

ibn-al-mujawir.name: Ibn al-Mujawir
ibn-al-mujawir.summary: Yemeni historian, traveler and businessman (c. 1205–1292) who wrote an important travel chronicle on southern Arabia and Socotra. It is a key source for the region's economic history and popular life.

yehuda-alharizi.name: Yehuda Alharizi
yehuda-alharizi.summary: Rabbi, translator, poet and traveler active in al-Andalus, who died in Aleppo in 1225. He is known for the Tahkemoni, a collection of tales sometimes called the 'Hebrew Maqamat'.

rassid-dynasty.name: Rassid dynasty
rassid-dynasty.summary: Zaidi Shia dynasty of imams that ruled parts of Yemen from 897, blending religious and political authority until the monarchy's abolition in 1970.

sulayhid-dynasty.name: Sulayhid dynasty
sulayhid-dynasty.summary: Ismaili Shi'ite Arab dynasty that ruled most of Yemen from 1047, bringing peace and prosperity to the region and allying with the Fatimid Caliphate.

zurayid-dynasty.name: Zurayid dynasty
zurayid-dynasty.summary: A ruling dynasty based in Aden, Yemen, from 1083 to 1174, and Hafizi Isma'ili Shi'a followers of the Fatimid Caliphate; their lands were later taken by the Ayyubid dynasty.

ismailism.name: Ismailism
ismailism.summary: A denomination of Shia Islam, one of three alongside Twelver and Zaydi Islam, marked by its distinctive emphasis on the esoteric, hidden meaning of Islamic teaching.

saladin.name: Saladin
saladin.summary: Founder of the Ayyubid dynasty and first sultan of Egypt and Syria (c. 1137 to 1193), who led the Muslim military effort against the Crusader states during the Third Crusade.

mamluk.name: Mamluks
mamluk.summary: Non-Arab enslaved soldiers, often of Turkic or Circassian origin, who converted to Islam and trained for war before being freed to serve as an elite military and political class in Egypt for nearly 1,000 years.

tihamah.name: Tihamah
tihamah.summary: The Red Sea coastal plain of the Arabian Peninsula, running from the Gulf of Aqaba to the Bab el Mandeb strait.

ma-n-dynasty.name: Ma'n dynasty
ma-n-dynasty.summary: Family of Druze chiefs of Arab descent based in the Chouf area of Mount Lebanon, politically prominent from the 15th to 17th centuries.

kingdom-of-hormuz.name: Kingdom of Hormuz
kingdom-of-hormuz.summary: A trading kingdom on the Persian Gulf founded in the 11th century by a dynasty of Arab origin, controlling a key port between the Gulf and the Indian Ocean until becoming a Portuguese client state.

hejaz.name: Hejaz
hejaz.summary: A historical region of western Arabia, in modern Saudi Arabia, containing the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, the first and second holiest sites in Islam.

al-ashraf-isma-il-i.name: Al-Ashraf Isma'il I
al-ashraf-isma-il-i.summary: Seventh Rasulid sultan of Yemen, reigning 1377 to 1400, who continued his father's patronage of scholarship and wrote a general history of Yemen.

natan-el-al-fayyumi.name: Natan'el al-Fayyumi
natan-el-al-fayyumi.summary: A 12th-century Yemenite Jewish author (c. 1090–1165) who wrote the Judeo-Arabic philosophical work Garden of the Intellects, influenced by Ismaili Islam.

hoter-ben-shlomo.name: Hoter ben Shlomo
hoter-ben-shlomo.summary: Yemeni scholar and philosopher (c.1400–c.1480) influenced by Natan'el al-Fayyumi, Maimonides, Saadia Gaon and al-Ghazali, and author of the philosophical work 'Lamp of Intellects.'

maimonides.name: Maimonides
maimonides.summary: Sephardic Jewish rabbi (c. 1135/38-1204) widely seen as one of the most influential Torah scholars of the Middle Ages, who also served as physician to Saladin.

saadia-gaon.name: Saadia Gaon
saadia-gaon.summary: A rabbi, philosopher and scholar (892–942) active in the Abbasid Caliphate, known for pioneering Judeo-Arabic writing and integrating Jewish theology with Greek philosophy.

al-ghazali.name: Al-Ghazali
al-ghazali.summary: A Persian Sunni Muslim scholar and polymath (c. 1058-1111), regarded as one of Islamic history's most influential theologians, jurists and mystics.

brethren-of-purity.name: Brethren of Purity
brethren-of-purity.summary: Secret society, likely of Muslim philosophers based in Basra during the Buyid dynasty, whose esoteric teachings were expounded in a 52-epistle encyclopedia that influenced later works.

midrash-ha-hefez.name: Midrash ha-Hefez
midrash-ha-hefez.summary: A Hebrew midrash on the Pentateuch and other biblical books, written by physician and rabbi Zechariah ben Solomon ha-Rofé beginning in 1430 in Yemen.

zechariah-ha-rof.name: Zechariah ha-Rofé
zechariah-ha-rof.summary: A 15th-century Yemenite Jewish scholar and physician who wrote Midrash ha-Hefetz, a biblical commentary blending Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy with the teachings of Maimonides.

yaqut-al-hamawi.name: Yaqut al-Hamawi
yaqut-al-hamawi.summary: Muslim scholar of Byzantine ancestry (1179–1229), active in the late Abbasid period, known for his influential geographical dictionary Mu'jam al-Buldan.

hisham-ibn-al-kalbi.name: Hisham ibn al-Kalbi
hisham-ibn-al-kalbi.summary: An 8th-century Arab Muslim historian (737–819 CE) from Kufa who collected genealogies and history of the ancient Arabs, best known for his Book of Idols on pre-Islamic pagan worship.

book-of-idols.name: Book of Idols
book-of-idols.summary: An early Islamic-era work by Arab scholar Hisham ibn al-Kalbi (737–819) describing polytheistic worship in pre-Islamic Arabia, though modern historians doubt its reliability as a source.

julius-wellhausen.name: Julius Wellhausen
julius-wellhausen.summary: German biblical scholar and orientalist, 1844 to 1918, credited as an originator of the documentary hypothesis about the Torah's composition, who also studied early Islam.

al-bahrani.name: Al-Bahrani
al-bahrani.summary: Thirteenth-century Bahraini Twelver Shia theologian and philosopher (1238-1299), part of a Bahrain school of thought that blended rationalism with mysticism.

mahooz.name: Mahooz
mahooz.summary: Neighborhood in Manama, the capital of Bahrain, near which a 13th-century mystic's mosque and tomb can still be visited.

rashid-al-din-hamadani.name: Rashid al-Din Hamadani
rashid-al-din-hamadani.summary: Statesman, historian and physician in Ilkhanate Iran (1247–1318) who, as vizier, wrote the Jami al-Tawarikh, a key source on the Mongol Empire, before being executed.

jami-al-tawarikh.name: Jami' al-Tawarikh
jami-al-tawarikh.summary: Early 14th-century work often called 'the first world history,' written by Rashid al-Din for the Mongol Ilkhanate and covering cultures from China to Europe.

al-shahrastani.name: Al-Shahrastani
al-shahrastani.summary: A Persian historian of religions and theologian (1086–1153) whose book on sects and creeds pioneered an objective study of world religions.
